SOURCE ESSAY:
On the first of May I was sitting outside a café in the Place de la Bastille in Paris staring at the exultant column, crowned with a capering figure, which stands in the place where the people destroyed a prison and ended an age. The thing is a curious example of how symbolic is the great part of human history. As a matter of mere material fact, the Bastille when it was taken was not a horrible prison; it was hardly a prison at all. But it was a symbol, and the people always go by a sure instinct for symbols; for the Chinaman, for instance, at the last General Election, or for President Kruger’s hat in the election before; their poetic sense is perfect. The Chinaman with his pigtail is not an idle flippancy. He does typify with a compact precision exactly the thing the people resent in African policy, the alien and grotesque nature of the power of wealth, the fact that money has no roots, that it is not a natural and familiar power, but a sort of airy and evil magic calling monsters from the ends of the earth. The people hate the mine owner who can bring a Chinaman flying across the sea, exactly as the people hated the wizard who could fetch a flying dragon through the air. It was the same with Mr. Kruger’s hat. His hat (that admirable hat) was not merely a joke. It did symbolise, and symbolise extremely well, the exact thing which our people at that moment regarded with impatience and venom; the old-fashioned, dingy, Republican simplicity, the unbeautiful dignity of the bourgeois, and the heavier truisms of political morality. No; the people are sometimes wrong on the practical side of politics; they are never wrong on the artistic side.

.....

So it was, certainly, with the Bastille. The destruction of the Bastille was not a reform; it was something more important than a reform. It was an iconoclasm; it was the breaking of a stone image. The people saw the building like a giant looking at them with a score of eyes, and they struck at it as at a carved fact. For of all the shapes in which that immense illusion called materialism can terrify the soul, perhaps the most oppressive are big buildings. Man feels like a fly, an accident, in the thing he has himself made. It requires a violent effort of the spirit to remember that man made this confounding thing and man could unmake it. Therefore the mere act of the ragged people in the street taking and destroying a huge public building has a spiritual, a ritual meaning far beyond its immediate political results. It is a religious service. If, for instance, the Socialists were numerous or courageous enough to capture and smash up the Bank of England, you might argue for ever about the inutility of the act, and how it really did not touch the root of the economic problem in the correct manner. But mankind would never forget it. It would change the world.

Architecture is a very good test of the true strength of a society, for the most valuable things in a human state are the irrevocable things—marriage, for instance. And architecture approaches nearer than any other art to being irrevocable, because it is so difficult to get rid of. You can turn a picture with its face to the wall; it would be a nuisance to turn that Roman cathedral with its face to the wall. You can tear a poem to pieces; it is only in moments of very sincere emotion that you tear a town-hall to pieces. A building is akin to dogma; it is insolent, like a dogma. Whether or no it is permanent, it claims permanence like a dogma. People ask why we have no typical architecture of the modern world, like impressionism in painting. Surely it is obviously because we have not enough dogmas; we cannot bear to see anything in the sky that is solid and enduring, anything in the sky that does not change like the clouds of the sky. But along with this decision which is involved in creating a building, there goes a quite similar decision in the more delightful task of smashing one. The two of necessity go together. In few places have so many fine public buildings been set up as here in Paris, and in few places have so many been destroyed. When people have finally got into the horrible habit of preserving buildings, they have got out of the habit of building them. And in London one mingles, as it were, one’s tears because so few are pulled down.

.....

As I sat staring at the column of the Bastille, inscribed to Liberty and Glory, there came out of one corner of the square (which, like so many such squares, was at once crowded and quiet) a sudden and silent line of horsemen. Their dress was of a dull blue, plain and prosaic enough, but the sun set on fire the brass and steel of their helmets; and their helmets were carved like the helmets of the Romans. I had seen them by twos and threes often enough before. I had seen plenty of them in pictures toiling through the snows of Friedland or roaring round the squares at Waterloo. But now they came file after file, like an invasion, and something in their numbers, or in the evening light that lit up their faces and their crests, or something in the reverie into which they broke, made me inclined to spring to my feet and cry out, “The French soldiers!” There were the little men with the brown faces that had so often ridden through the capitals of Europe as coolly as they now rode through their own. And when I looked across the square I saw that the two other corners were choked with blue and red; held by little groups of infantry. The city was garrisoned as against a revolution.

Of course, I had heard all about the strike, chiefly from a baker. He said he was not going to “Chomer.” I said, “Qu’est-ce que c’est que le chome?” He said, “Ils ne veulent pas travailler.” I said, “Ni moi non plus,” and he thought I was a class-conscious collectivist proletarian. The whole thing was curious, and the true moral of it one not easy for us, as a nation, to grasp, because our own faults are so deeply and dangerously in the other direction. To me, as an Englishman (personally steeped in the English optimism and the English dislike of severity), the whole thing seemed a fuss about nothing. It looked like turning out one of the best armies in Europe against ordinary people walking about the street. The cavalry charged us once or twice, more or less harmlessly. But, of course, it is hard to say how far in such criticisms one is assuming the French populace to be (what it is not) as docile as the English. But the deeper truth of the matter tingled, so to speak, through the whole noisy night. This people has a natural faculty for feeling itself on the eve of something—of the Bartholomew or the Revolution or the Commune or the Day of Judgment. It is this sense of crisis that makes France eternally young. It is perpetually pulling down and building up, as it pulled down the prison and put up the column in the Place de La Bastille. France has always been at the point of dissolution. She has found the only method of immortality. She dies daily.

message.content:
On the first of May, I found myself seated at an outdoor café in the Place de la Bastille, gazing at the jubilant column topped with a lively figure. This monument stands where a prison was razed, marking the end of an era. It serves as a fascinating illustration of the symbolic nature of much of human history. In terms of physical reality, the Bastille was not a particularly dreadful prison; in fact, it was barely a prison at all. However, it represented something far greater, and people have a remarkable instinct for recognizing these symbols. Take, for instance, the figure of the Chinaman during the last General Election, or President Kruger’s hat in the previous election; the public's poetic sensibility is uncanny. The Chinaman, identifiable by his pigtail, is not a mere triviality. He encapsulates precisely what the populace resents about African policy: the foreign and absurd nature of wealth's power, the notion that money lacks roots and is not an inherent or familiar force, but an almost sinister magic that summons monsters from distant lands. The public loathes the mine owner who can effortlessly transport a Chinaman across the ocean, just as they detested the sorcerer who could conjure a dragon to fly through the air. Similarly, Mr. Kruger’s hat, which was quite remarkable, was not simply a source of humor. It adeptly symbolized what people were feeling at that moment—impatience and disdain for the outdated, drab Republican simplicity, the unremarkable dignity of the bourgeoisie, and the weighty clichés of political morality. While the masses may sometimes err in practical political matters, they are never mistaken when it comes to the artistic dimension.

This notion surely applies to the Bastille. The act of demolishing the Bastille was more than a mere reform; it was an act of iconoclasm, a shattering of a stone idol. The populace perceived the edifice as a giant with numerous eyes, and they struck it as if attacking a tangible fact. Among the many manifestations of materialism that can oppress the human spirit, few are as stifling as monumental structures. Individuals often feel insignificant, as if they are mere accidents within the very creations of their own hands. It requires a strenuous mental effort to recall that humanity constructed these formidable buildings and, in theory, has the power to dismantle them. Consequently, the mere act of the ragged masses taking down a massive public structure carries a spiritual and ritualistic significance that far surpasses its immediate political implications. It resembles a sacred rite. If, for instance, a courageous and numerous group of Socialists were to seize and demolish the Bank of England, one could debate the futility of such an act endlessly, arguing that it fails to address the root of the economic issue correctly. Yet, humanity would not forget it. Such an act would alter the world.

Architecture serves as an excellent gauge of a society's true vitality, as the most cherished aspects of a community are those that are irrevocable—marriage being one example. Architecture comes closer than most other art forms to achieving this permanence, given its inherent difficulty in being removed. One can easily turn a painting to face the wall; however, it would be quite a chore to rotate a grand Roman cathedral in the same way. While one can shred a poem, tearing down a town hall is typically reserved for moments of profound emotion. A structure stands as a form of dogma, asserting itself with an insolent permanence, much like a dogmatic belief. People often wonder why contemporary society lacks a distinctive architectural style akin to the impressionism found in painting. The answer is quite apparent; we lack sufficient dogmas. We are uncomfortable with anything solid and enduring that occupies the sky, preferring instead the ephemeral nature of clouds. Yet, the decision to construct a building carries with it a similar resolve to the more delightful task of demolishing one. These two actions are inherently linked. In Paris, there are numerous magnificent public buildings, and yet, there have also been many that were destroyed. When a society becomes accustomed to preserving structures, it often loses the habit of creating them. In London, one finds oneself shedding tears for the few buildings that are taken down.

As I continued to gaze at the Bastille's column, inscribed with the words of Liberty and Glory, a sudden line of horsemen emerged from one corner of the square, which, like many such public spaces, was both crowded and serene. Their attire was a plain, dull blue, but the sunlight ignited the brass and steel of their helmets, which were designed like those worn by Roman soldiers. I had seen these soldiers in smaller numbers before, and I had encountered many images of them, trudging through the snow at Friedland or charging through the squares at Waterloo. However, now they advanced in tight formation, and something about their numbers, combined with the evening light illuminating their faces and crests, stirred a feeling that compelled me to leap to my feet and shout, “The French soldiers!” There they were—the small men with brown faces who had so often traversed the capitals of Europe as effortlessly as they now navigated their own streets. Glancing across the square, I noticed that the other corners were congested with blue and red, held by groups of infantry. The city was fortified against a potential uprising.

I had certainly heard about the strike, primarily from a local baker. He expressed his refusal to “Chomer.” I inquired, “Qu’est-ce que c’est que le chome?” He replied, “Ils ne veulent pas travailler.” I responded with, “Ni moi non plus,” which led him to mistakenly assume I was a class-conscious collectivist. The whole situation was intriguing, and the genuine lesson it offered is not one that is easily grasped by us as a nation, given our own deep-rooted tendencies that often lean in the opposite direction. As an Englishman, raised in an environment steeped in optimism and a reluctance to embrace severity, I found the entire affair to seem like a fuss over trivial matters. It appeared as though one of the finest armies in Europe was being mobilized against ordinary citizens merely going about their day. The cavalry charged at us a few times, yet the encounters were relatively harmless. However, it is challenging to discern how much of my critique is based on an assumption that the French populace is as docile as the English, which it is not. Yet, amidst the tumult of that noisy night, a deeper truth resonated. This people possesses an innate ability to sense that they are on the brink of something monumental—whether it be the Bartholomew, the Revolution, the Commune, or the Day of Judgment. It is this acute awareness of crisis that keeps France eternally youthful. The nation is in a constant cycle of destruction and creation, having once demolished a prison to erect the column in the Place de La Bastille. France has consistently been on the verge of collapse. Yet, in this cycle of renewal, she has discovered her method of immortality, for she dies anew each day.
